messages.content: Build-Measure-Learn: minimise the loop between idea and validated learning. Build the minimum viable product (MVP) — the smallest thing that tests your most critical assumption. Measure: define in advance what constitutes evidence that your hypothesis is correct or wrong. Learn: update your understanding, pivot or persevere. Pivot: structured change in strategy (customer segment, problem, solution, revenue model) based on learning. Key insight: the goal is not to execute your plan — the goal is to discover what plan is worth executing. Most initial plans are wrong; the methodology makes being wrong cheap and fast.
How do you evaluate whether an innovation is genuinely valuable?

Test against: Does it solve a real problem people currently have (not a hypothetical future problem)? Is the problem painful enough that people pay to solve it now, rather than a nice-to-have? Is the solution meaningfully better than what already exists — 10x better, not 10% better? Can it be delivered at a price point users will pay and at a cost that allows a sustainable business? Will network effects, switching costs, or other dynamics make it defensible? False signals: people say they'd buy it (verbal intent ≠ actual purchase), existing users love it (early adopters ≠ mainstream market).

Clayton Christensen's insight: well-managed, customer-focused companies fail because they are too well-managed and too customer-focused. They invest in what current customers want today, which is always the existing product, improved. Disruptive technology targets different customers initially. Rational to ignore. By the time existing customers want the new technology, the disruptor has won. The dilemma: the very practices that create success prevent companies from pursuing disruptive innovations. Solution: run separate organisational units for disruptive bets, isolated from the core business's resource allocation processes.
